## 1. Exponential growth equation

We will start with a simple example of exponential growth. Think about a hypothetical population that starts with 2 individuals. Let's imagine the population size doubles every year ($\lambda=2$) and has distinct generations. Therefore, we will model discrete population growth, rather than continuous population growth. We will simulate 10 generations (time = 10). How large will the population be in year 10? Below I first set up a few variables:

**N0** is the population size at time zero.

**lambda** ($\lambda$) is the population growth rate. Sometimes I'll call this 'R' for convience. When ($\lambda (or R)>1$), the population size increases. When ($\lambda (or R)<1$) the population size decreases.

**time** (t) is the number of years we want data for.

**Nt** is the population at times (t).

Then I set up the exponential growth equation for discrete population growth:

$N_{t+1} = N_t * \lambda$.

Another way to write this equation, which is more convient to code in R is:

$N_t = N_0 * \lambda^t$.

The vector **Nt** is an object that we create to catch the results of the equation on the right-hand side of the \<-.

```{r , echo=T}
## lines 3-10 in associated R code
NO <- 2
lambda <- 2
time <- 0:10

Nt <- NO * lambda**time

ggplot(data=NULL,aes(x=time, y=Nt)) + geom_point(size=2) + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

How large is the population in year 10? In the R code, change $\lambda$ to see how it affects the population size at time 10.

### Three populations, each with a different starting size

Now we will look at the effect of changing the starting population size. The code below simulates three populations at size $N_0$ = 10, 20, and 40.

```{r , echo=T}
## lines 13-22 in associated R code

N0 <- c(10,20,40) 
lambda <- 2
time <- 0:5

Nt.s <- sapply(N0, function(n) n * lambda**time) %>% as.data.frame() %>% cbind(time) %>% pivot_longer(cols=1:3, names_to = 'group', values_to = 'N')

## Population sizes for the six years
ggplot(data=Nt.s, aes(x=time, y=N, color=group)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()

```

Now plot the data on the $log_{10}$ scale.

```{r, echo=T}
## Population sizes for the six years on $log_{10}$ scale
ggplot(data=Nt.s, aes(x=time, y=N, color=group)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + scale_y_log10() + theme_bw()
```

How do these three populations differ? What is the effect of starting population size? What is the effect of plotting $log_{10} (N_t)$

### Three populations, each with a different lambdas

Now we will look at the effect of changing the population growth rate ($\lambda$). The code below simulates three populations at $\lambda =$ 0.5, 1, and 1.

```{r , echo=T}
## lines 25-34 in associated R code
N0 <- 100 
lambdas <- c(0.7, 1, 1.5)
time <- 0:5

Nt.all <- sapply(lambdas, function(x) N0 * x**time) %>% as.data.frame() %>% cbind(time) %>% pivot_longer(cols=1:3, names_to = 'group', values_to = 'N')

## Population sizes for the six years 
ggplot(data=Nt.all, aes(x=time, y=N, color=group)) + geom_point(size=2) + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

Now plot the data on the $log_{10}$ scale.

```{r, echo=T}
## Population sizes for the six years on $log_{10}$ scale
ggplot(data=Nt.all, aes(x=time, y=N, color=group)) + geom_point(size=2) + geom_line() + scale_y_log10() + theme_bw()
```

How do these three populations differ? What is the effect of lambda? What makes a bigger difference in population size after five years, changing lambda from 1.5 to 2 or changing initial population size from 20 to 100?

## 2. Miami blue population dynamics example

The Miami blue *Cyclargus thomasi bethunbakeri* is an endangered species in Florida. It was once widespread and occurred throughout much of south Florida, but now only one small population remains in a preserve. Read more about the biology [here](http://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/bfly/miami_blue.htm).

![Miami blue butterflies. credit:J.Gage](miami-blue-170302-0336.jpg)

Below are data for population size counts for a the endangered miami blue butterfly. We have 21 years of data where researchers counted the butterflies at several sites across their range. The values are estimated population size each year. Please note that these are **hypothetical data** that I simulated and do not reflect actual abundances of the butterfly. [Read more](https://www.floridastateparks.org/learn/saving-miami-blue-butterfly-0) about conservation actions being taken by the Daniels Lab here at UF and watch the [video](https://youtu.be/d1NDRgPG4kQ).

```{r , echo=F}
## lines 38-58 in associated R code
year <- 0:20
set.seed(5)
Count <- abs(round(rnorm(21, (100*1.05^year), 70),0))
dat <- as.data.frame(cbind(year,Count))

ggplot(data=dat, aes(x=year, y=Count)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

Calculate the rate of increase ($\lambda$ or R) for each year-to-year transition.

```{r, echo=T, warning=F}
dat$obs.R <- NA

dat$obs.R[2:21] <- dat$Count[2:21]/dat$Count[1:20]
obs.R <- dat$Count[2:21]/dat$Count[1:20]

ggplot(data=dat, aes(x=year, y=obs.R)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept=1,lty=2) + theme_bw()
```

The dashed on the graph above shows $\lambda = 1$, so above the line the population size will increase and below the line the population size will decrease.

Plot R against the population density

```{r, echo=T, warning=F}
ggplot(data=NULL, aes(x=dat$Count[1:20], y=obs.R)) + geom_point() + geom_abline(intercept=1,slope=0, linetype="dashed") + 
  labs(x="Population density",y="observed R")+ theme_bw()
```

### 2a. Project out population size estimates for 50 years

We know the population size and the rates of increase/decrease for 20 transitions. Now we want to know what the popualtion size might be in 50 years. Will it substantially increase? Is there a chance the Miami blue will go extinct?

We can answer these questions by randomly sampling from our list of 20 R's. We do this 50 times to simulate population dynamics for 50 years. What density should we start the simulation? We could pick the average density (\~100) or the minimum (22). Let's be conservative and start our simulated population at the minimum of 22 butterflies.

```{r , echo=F}
## lines 62-75 in associated R code
years <- 0:50 #setup a vector for years from 0 to 50
set.seed(1)   # set seed for the randomization so we can reproduce the randomized results
sim.Rs <- sample(x = obs.R, size = 50, replace = TRUE) # this line randomly samples values from 'obs.R' 50 times with replacement

out50yr <- numeric(length(years))
out50yr[1] <- min(dat$Count) 

for (t in 1:50) out50yr[t + 1] <- {
  out50yr[t] * sim.Rs[t]
  }

ggplot(data=NULL, aes(x=years, y=out50yr)) + labs(y="count") + geom_point() + geom_line() + theme_bw()

```

Booming! How many butterflies might there be in 50 years?

This is just one random simulation. We might want to do many versions of this simulation to get an idea of how variables these results might be. Try removing the **set.seed(1)** on line 64 in the associated R code by inserting a **\#** at the start of the line. It should turn green and "turn it off". Now run the chunk of code from line 63-75. Each run is a new simulation. What do you see?

### 2b. function for running many 50 year simulations

Let's create a function that will do the above randomization a bunch of times.

```{r, echo=T, warning=F}
## lines 78-89 in associated R code
PopSim <- function(Rs, N0, years = 50, sims = 1) {
  sim.RM = matrix(sample(Rs, size = sims * years, replace = TRUE),
                    nrow = years, ncol = sims)
  output <- numeric(years + 1)
  output[1] <- N0
  outmat <- sapply(1:sims, function(i) {
    for (t in 1:years) output[t + 1] <- round(output[t] * sim.RM[t, i], 0)
    output
    })
  return(outmat)
  }
```

Now we have the function **'PopSim'** that can run a bunch of these simulations for us. Let's start with 10 by setting 'sims=10' in the function below.

```{r, echo=T, warning=F}
## lines 92-100 in associated R code
sim10 <- as.data.frame(PopSim(Rs = obs.R, N0 = 43, sims = 10)) %>% mutate(year=0:50) %>%  gather("sim","count",-year)

# plot the 10 simulated populations
ggplot(sim10, aes(x=year,y=count,color=sim))+geom_line() + theme_bw()

```

What do we see? Are they all the same? Why or why not?

Some of the populations are so big that it's hard to see the patterns for some of the populations. Let's take the *ln* of the count. Note that I've added 1 to the count because you can't take log of 0. Additionally, $ln(1)=0$, so zeros will remain zeros but very high values will be condensed. This transformation allows us to visualize the data more clearly on the graph.

```{r, echo=T}
ggplot(sim10, aes(x=year,y=log(count+1),color=sim))+geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

Note that because we are randomly sampling the R's with replacement, your 10 populations might show different dynamics than this graph.

```{r, echo=T, warning=F, message=F}
ggplot(data=sim10 %>% filter(year==50), aes(x=log(count+1)))+geom_histogram()
```

Here is another way to visualize the data. This shows the counts at the end of the simluation in year 50.

Finally, let's calculate a few summaries of the estimated counts at the end of our simluations in year 50. In the code below, I subsetting the simulated data to include only year 50.

**year50_quantiles** is the 90% quantile range. If we do enough simluations, these values are equivilent to the 90% confidence intervals. Essentially 90% of our simulated population sizes in year 50 should be within that range.

**n_extinct** counts up the number of populations of size zero in year 50. So, simulated populations that went extinct.

```{r, echo=T, warning=F}
simsummary <- sim10 %>% filter(year==50) %>% select(count) 
year50_quantiles <- quantile(simsummary$count, probs=c(.05,.95))
n_extinct <- sim10 %>% filter(year==50 & count==0) %>% count() %>% as.data.frame()
```

```{r, echo=T}
year50_quantiles
```

```{r, echo=T}
n_extinct
```

What can we learn from the 10 simulations based on the last two figures? Do any populations go extinct? Re-run line 91 and remake the plots. Do things change? How much?

Run 100 simulations and estimate year50_quantiles and n_extinct. Are these estimates reasonable? Complete questions on canvas.
